Reprove

/rih-PROOV/ - rhymes with approve · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Reprove means to scold or correct, usually gently.

With one raised eyebrow and two soft words, the conductor reproved the trombones for rushing.

Worked Example

The ranger caught the family mid-toss, peanuts arcing toward the squirrels. She did not raise her voice or reach for the citation pad. She named what the food does to a wild animal's winter instincts, thanked them for hearing her out, and walked on. The peanuts went back in the pack, and the family waved to her later from the trailhead.

Reprove is the exact word for what she did, because it means to scold or correct, usually gently — disapproval made unmistakable while everyone's dignity stays intact. Scold runs hotter and louder and often just vents; a reproof aims to fix the behavior, and it usually does.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — remind → reprove → chew out

remind vs. reprove

remind vs. reprove: Remind carries no criticism at all — just a nudge that the rule exists.

chew out vs. reprove

chew out vs. reprove: Chew out goes further than reprove — the volume rises and the anger shows, while a reproof stays gentle enough to thank someone for afterward.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: the reverse of

Root — prove

Root — prove: to test, to find good (Latin probare)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (expressing reversal) + prove (to test and find good) = to find NOT good — and to say so, usually gently. Approve and reprove are mirror twins from Latin probare: one announces the test was passed, the other that it was not. Reprobate, this unit's harsher sibling, carries the same reversed root to a final judgment on character.

Use the root in a new word: approve

Use the root in a new word: approve: The board voted to approve the design — tested it and found it good, prov-'s happier answer.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / gentle

Reprove is correction with the volume down — disapproval made plain, dignity intact. Scold runs hotter; correct has no feelings in it at all. In this unit's disapproval family, each word takes a different object: reprove a person, gently, for an act; repudiate a claim or belief, formally and entirely; repulse a physical advance; and save reprobate for the character past correcting. If the correction could plausibly end with a thank-you, it was a reproof.
